title: How Tap to Pay Actually Works

sections.name: Hook
lines: tp_hook
Your bank card has no battery. So how does it talk to the card reader? The reader powers it, through thin air.
tp_title
Here's what happens in that one-second tap, in five steps.

sections.name: Power from the reader
lines: tp_field
Step one. The reader has a coil of wire that makes a magnetic field, flipping thirteen and a half million times a second.
tp_coil
Inside your card, a thin loop of wire runs around the edge. Bring it close, and that field makes a current flow in it.
tp_wake
That tiny current is enough to wake up the chip. It's why you have to hold the card so close, just a few centimetres.

sections.name: Talking back
lines: tp_talk
Step two. The chip replies by flickering how much power it draws. The reader feels those flickers, and reads them as data.
tp_nfc
This short-range chat is called NFC, near field communication. It only works over a few centimetres, on purpose.

sections.name: A one-time code
lines: tp_code
Step three. The chip doesn't just send your card number. It creates a one-time code, just for this payment.
tp_reuse
Copy that code and try it again, and it's useless. That's what makes contactless cards so hard to clone.

sections.name: Phones and watches
lines: tp_token
Step four. Your phone doesn't even store your real card number. It keeps a stand-in number, called a token.
tp_unlock
And it only pays after your face, fingerprint or passcode says it's really you.
tp_watch
Watches and payment rings work the same way, with a tiny antenna and chip tucked inside.

sections.name: The approval
lines: tp_bank
Step five. The reader sends the details through the payment network to your bank, which checks your account and says yes or no.
tp_pin
For bigger amounts, many cards ask for your PIN as well, as an extra check.
tp_beep
That whole round trip usually takes a second or two. Then, beep.

sections.name: Recap
lines: w_recap
The reader powers the card. The chip flickers back a one-time code. Phones use a token, and your bank says yes.
outro
Next time you tap, remember, a magnet just powered a tiny computer. Follow for more of the tech you use every day.
